title: Static habitat adjustment cut the spatial thermal slope by 73% at 217 English river sites
abstract: We tested whether a spatial temperature benchmark in English river invertebrates also described habitat differences. We used 3,715 autumn samples at 217 sites, trained community axes on 1991–2000 records, and tested spatial slopes on held-out sites and annual slopes in 2001–2017. With the score and sites fixed, adjustment for channel habitat and upstream land cover reduced the spatial temperature slope from 0.925 to 0.251, a 73% reduction (central 95% crossed site-and-year resampling range 59–90%). The annual slope stayed at 0.058 by design. Its point ratio rose from 6.3% to 23.2% through the denominator alone. Physical habitat controls gave a 58% reduction before land cover was added. The fixed BOD slope fell by 59%, but its adjusted denominator was unstable. A thermal axis trained with all habitat controls gave a spatial slope of 0.316 and annual slope of 0.030; its denominator was non-positive in 35 of 399 resamples. These records thus do not establish a precise residual tracking rate. Habitat covariation accounts for much of this spatial benchmark, but adjustment is descriptive. Mixed descriptor dates, a 2015 land-cover snapshot, air rather than water temperature, family records and resampling bias limit causal interpretation. Code, aggregate results and exact external input hashes permit reproduction without bundling external databases.

display.caption: Static habitat adjustment reduced the spatial temperature and BOD slopes on fixed community scores. Bars show central 95% ranges from 399 crossed site-and-year resamples. Annual models and scores stay fixed across columns.
